opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to approach this is to look backward before looking forward. If you go back over the history of AI, you see a series of capability unlocks: playing games like chess and Go, then image recognition, then fairly fluent language, then coding and reasoning at a level that's genuinely useful. A useful exercise is to ask, roughly, how much effective compute did each of those unlocks take, and how many orders of magnitude separated one from the next?

When you do that, a pattern comes out. A lot of these transitions happened over something like a few orders of magnitude of scaling in training compute, combined with algorithmic progress that effectively multiplies that compute. Historically, frontier training compute has grown by something like four to five times per year, and algorithmic efficiency has improved at a comparable rate on top of that. So you're getting a large number of effective orders of magnitude per decade.

Then the question becomes: how much more do we need to get to something like fully automating remote work? That means an agent that can take a vague goal, operate a computer, coordinate with people, recover from mistakes, and work coherently over days or weeks rather than minutes. My honest view is that there's a lot of uncertainty here, so I don't want to give a point estimate. I think of it as a distribution over how many more orders of magnitude you need. If you take the historical record seriously, each major qualitative unlock has needed a handful of extra orders of magnitude. And there are some things we clearly don't have yet: long-horizon agency, reliable multimodal computer use, and the kind of robust common sense that lets you hand someone a messy task and walk away. It would be a bit surprising if all of that dropped out of the very next scale-up. It would also be surprising if it took, say, twenty more orders of magnitude.

So you end up with a fairly wide distribution. Some meaningful probability mass lands within the next decade, but there's a long tail.

The other crucial piece is the economics, which I think people underweight. Even partial automation of remote work is enormously valuable. Remote-able tasks are a big chunk of the economy, tens of trillions of dollars a year in wages globally. So as systems get closer, the incentive to pour more compute, more chips, and more talent into the problem grows, and that can accelerate the scaling itself. On the other hand, there are physical constraints: fabs, energy, data center buildout, data availability. Those put some brakes on how fast you can add orders of magnitude.

Putting it together, I'd say compute scaling and the historical track record give you the backbone of the forecast. The economic feedback loops and the physical bottlenecks tell you how fast you move along it. And the thing I'd caution against is anchoring too hard on vibes from the latest model release, in either direction. The trend lines have been remarkably more predictive than people's intuitions.

r001.rationale: It says major capability transitions historically took “a few orders of magnitude” of training-compute scaling, which conveys roughly three orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It lists missing competencies, but frames the distance to remote-work automation as a distribution over additional orders of magnitude, not over how many further major competencies AI must acquire.

r003.rationale: It gives the historical annual pace of compute growth and explains that economic feedback and physical bottlenecks determine how fast systems move along the forecast trajectory.

r004.rationale: It discusses the economic value of remote-work automation and investment incentives, but does not estimate that three or four further orders of magnitude would make infrastructure investment a nontrivial fraction of world output.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about this is essentially a kind of extrapolation exercise, but one where you try to be disciplined about what you're extrapolating and what you're assuming along the way.

The starting point is that we have a pretty good picture of how training compute has grown over the past decade or so. Frontier training runs have been scaling at roughly four to five times per year, and that's been remarkably consistent. On top of that, you have algorithmic progress, which effectively acts like additional compute. Our estimates suggest that algorithmic improvements have roughly doubled the effective compute budget every year or so, maybe a bit faster. So when you combine the two, you get a very steep trajectory in what I'd call effective compute, the thing that actually drives capabilities.

The second piece is linking that effective compute to capabilities. And here you can look at a bunch of benchmarks and ask, how much effective compute did it take to go from, say, roughly high-school level performance on some task to roughly expert level? And across a range of domains, it tends to take something on the order of a few orders of magnitude. That gives you a kind of exchange rate between compute and capability, which is admittedly noisy, but it's not nothing.

Then the hard part is figuring out how far current systems are from being able to do remote work in general. And I think the honest answer is that we don't have great benchmarks for this. The things we measure well are relatively short, well-specified tasks, and remote work is mostly about long-horizon, messy, context-dependent tasks where you need to coordinate with other people and remember what happened last week and so on. One thing we've been trying to do is look at the length of tasks that models can reliably complete, measured in terms of how long it would take a human, and that's been growing fairly quickly, something like doubling every several months. If you take that trend seriously and ask when it crosses the threshold of, say, tasks that take a person a week or a month, you get answers that are not that far out, maybe within a decade.

But I'd put pretty wide error bars on this. The extrapolation could break because the remaining gaps are qualitatively different, things like continual learning or genuine agency over long periods, and it's not obvious that just scaling the current recipe closes them. And it could break on the input side, because sustaining four or five times per year compute growth gets hard once you're talking about tens or hundreds of billions of dollars per training run and serious constraints on power and chips. So my view is that the trends point toward automation of a large fraction of remote work being plausible within something like the next ten to fifteen years, but I think of that as a reasoned central estimate rather than a confident forecast.

r001.rationale: The response says expert-level performance across domains can take a few orders of magnitude of effective compute, but does not estimate major capability unlocks as occurring about once per three orders of training-compute scaling.

r002.rationale: It discusses task-length limits and possible gaps such as continual learning and agency, but does not frame the distance to human-level remote work in terms of how many additional major competencies AI must acquire.

r003.rationale: It notes that sustaining 4–5× annual compute growth may become difficult, but does not connect that condition to extrapolating the historical calendar pace of capability unlocks.

r004.rationale: It mentions training runs costing tens or hundreds of billions of dollars and constraints on power and chips, but gives no estimate of three or four further orders of magnitude of scaling or a fraction of world output.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by separating two questions: how much capability do we get from additional compute, and how much capability do we need to automate remote work? Historical progress gives us some evidence about the first. The second is much harder.

You can look at successive generations of models and ask how performance changes as training compute increases. Then, given assumptions about how quickly compute grows and algorithms improve, you can project that trend forward. But a benchmark score doesn’t translate directly into a fraction of jobs automated. A job involves many tasks, and being good at most of them may still leave you unable to do the job without supervision.

So the evidence I’d most want is how systems perform on representative work that takes humans different amounts of time. Can they reliably complete something that takes a person ten minutes, an hour, or a week? Can they handle ambiguity, notice mistakes, and recover without someone intervening? If we can measure how those abilities improve across model generations, we have a more useful basis for extrapolation.

The crucial uncertainty is whether those trends continue as we move toward longer, more complex work. Past advances make further substantial progress plausible, but they don’t, by themselves, establish a date for automating remote work. I’d use them to construct a range of forecasts, with explicit assumptions about compute, algorithmic progress, and reliability, rather than infer a single deadline from a scaling curve.

r001.rationale: It discusses capability changes with increased training compute, but gives no estimate that major capability unlocks occur about once per three orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It describes remote work as many tasks and asks whether systems can handle different work durations, but does not frame the distance to human-level performance as a number of additional major competencies.

r003.rationale: It says projections depend on assumptions about compute growth and algorithmic improvement, but does not explain that extrapolating the calendar pace of past unlocks requires sustaining the rapid compute growth that accompanied them.

r004.rationale: It makes no estimate connecting three or four more orders of magnitude of compute scaling to infrastructure spending as a fraction of world output.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful starting point is to ask how much progress we’ve seen for a given increase in training compute, and then ask how far that progress has actually taken us toward doing economically valuable work.

Those are two different questions. We have fairly good evidence that increasing compute improves model capabilities across a broad range of tasks. But translating that into a date for automating remote work requires knowing where the relevant threshold is. A model can perform very well on a benchmark and still struggle to carry out a project that takes a human several days, involves ambiguous instructions, and requires recovering from mistakes.

So I’d look at historical models and measure the kinds of work they can complete reliably, ideally using tasks drawn from actual jobs. Then I’d ask how that changes with training compute. If successive increases in compute let systems handle longer, more complex tasks, you can extrapolate that relationship and compare it with the compute we expect future training runs to use.

The big uncertainty is whether that relationship continues as you move toward whole jobs. Remote work is a bundle of activities, and automating most individual tasks doesn’t necessarily mean you can automate the job. You might still need a person to supply context, check the output, or intervene when something goes wrong.

So compute scaling gives you a way to discipline the forecast. It tells you something about the pace of capability improvement. But it doesn’t, by itself, tell you how far away automation is. For that, you need a credible measure of the remaining gap between what models can reliably do and what a remote worker actually does.

r001.rationale: The response discusses capability gains from increasing compute, but gives no estimate of a major capability unlock per three orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It describes the gap between models and remote work, but does not frame that distance as the number of additional major competencies AI must acquire.

r003.rationale: It suggests extrapolating capability gains against future compute, but does not connect historical calendar pace to sustaining rapid compute growth.

r004.rationale: It gives no estimate of compute scaling that would make infrastructure investment a fraction of world output.
